claims.claim: Care is delivered across a continuum of settings that differ in the acuity of illness they handle, their clinical function, and the payment context that reimburses them.

Ambulatory (outpatient) care is care for patients who are not admitted for an overnight stay, delivered in settings such as physician offices, clinics, hospital outpatient centers, and specialized centers.

Under 42 CFR 416.2, an ambulatory surgical center is a distinct entity operating exclusively to provide surgical services to patients not requiring hospitalization, where the expected duration of services would not exceed 24 hours following an admission.

Medicare describes skilled care as nursing and therapy care that can only be safely and effectively performed by, or under the supervision of, professional or technical personnel, and defines a skilled nursing facility as a nursing facility with the staff and equipment to give skilled nursing care and usually skilled rehabilitative services.

Medicare coverage of a skilled nursing facility stay generally requires a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least 3 days in a row, and time spent under observation or in the emergency department before formal inpatient admission does not count toward it.

A long-term care hospital is classified under 42 CFR 412.23(e) by having an average Medicare inpatient length of stay greater than 25 days; the same regulation separately classifies rehabilitation hospitals/units and psychiatric hospitals.

Home health is a range of skilled health care services delivered in the patient's own home for an illness or injury, and Medicare covers it for eligible patients who are largely confined to home and need intermittent skilled care.
Hospice is end-of-life care for people with illnesses that cannot be cured, organized around a plan of care set by the patient, family, and hospice team.

Telehealth is medical or health services delivered by a provider located elsewhere using audio and video communication technology, or audio-only communication in some cases, and can include office visits, psychotherapy, consultations, e-visits, and virtual check-ins.

The Institute of Medicine (1996) defines primary care as the provision of integrated, accessible health care services by clinicians accountable for addressing a large majority of personal health care needs, developing a sustained partnership with patients, and practicing in the context of family and community.

A levels-of-care framework ranks care by specialization and complexity: primary (first-contact, generalist), secondary (specialist, usually by referral), tertiary (highly specialized, complex hospital care), and quaternary (rare, advanced, or experimental care offered at a limited number of centers).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether 'ambulatory care' and 'outpatient care' are strictly synonymous.
positions: Common usage treats them as interchangeable: care without an overnight admission.
Some administrative usage reserves 'outpatient' for hospital-based departments and 'ambulatory' for free-standing settings.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats them as effectively synonymous for the introductory levels framework, while noting that the defining feature is the absence of an inpatient admission, not the building.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the 3-hour intensive-therapy expectation and the 60% compliance threshold belong in a definition of an inpatient rehabilitation facility.
positions: Those thresholds are widely cited features of IRFs.
They are set in CMS coverage and classification policy (Benefit Policy Manual and 42 CFR 412.29), not in the 412.23 hospital-classification text this lesson cites.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson describes IRFs functionally as providing intensive inpatient rehabilitation and does not assert the specific 3-hour or 60% figures as verified from the cited regulation.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Healthcare Delivery Settings is a foundational concept...') with no factual claims about actual care settings; all of it was discarded.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire boilerplate draft with sourced descriptions of each setting.
Added the levels-of-care framework and precise regulatory definitions for ASCs and LTCHs that the draft lacked.
Kept payment context at a high level (acuity/function/who-pays) to avoid crossing into billing mechanics owned by other topics.
rightsIssues: MedlinePlus, Medicare.gov, and the eCFR are U.S. government works used as REFERENCE_ONLY; facts were synthesized and rewritten in original prose, not copied.
The Keiser University article is a secondary university source used REFERENCE_ONLY to confirm the four-tier terminology; no wording was reproduced.

Used for framing the continuum; definitions synthesized, no wording copied.
